newsitem.title: USA: DuPont to invest $1.7 billion in Pioneer Hi-Bred.
newsitem.headline: DuPont to invest $1.7 billion in Pioneer Hi-Bred.

text.p: DuPont Co. said Thursday it will invest $1.7 billion for a 20 percent stake in agricultural company Pioneer Hi-Bred International Inc. as the two work to develop new, genetically enhanced crops.
The deal, which includes the formation of a joint venture and a research agreement, sent Pioneer shares up over 17 percent, as they gained $13.50 to $91.25 on the New York Stock Exchange.
"It positions (Pioneer) better in this new age of biotechnology in the sense that they're aligned now with a research giant," Prudential Securities analyst John McMillin said.
DuPont will pay $104 a share for 16 million shares of a new class of Pioneer stock. Pioneer, the largest North American seed corn company, will then buy back about 16 million shares from the public.

The joint venture company, Optimum Quality Grains, will include DuPont Agricultural Products' Quality Grains business and Pioneer's Nutrition Industry Markets business, both based in Des Moines, Iowa.

The companies said the alliance will create one of the world's largest private agricultural research and development collaborations. The two will collectively invest more than $400 million in agricultural research next year.

A portion of that money will support the joint venture directly, with collaborative research in genetic modification of corn, soybeans and other oilseeds to improve their oil, protein and carbohydrate composition.
The venture aims to have $100 million in sales in 1998 and $3.5 billion in 10 years, officials said.
The first line of products offered by the venture will be grains that can be used to make improved livestock feed to make healthier edible oils.

"(The products) are more valuable to the consumer or to feed livestock, which eventually goes to the consumer," said William Kirk, vice president and general manager of Du Pont Agricultural Products. "And we're sharing some of that value with farmers and others through the process."

Value-added crops are at the heart of the biotechnology revolution in agriculture. Agriculture firms are developing genetically enhanced crops that can fight off certain insects or withstand the use of certain herbicide chemicals to kill weeds in the field. Companies are also using genetics and biotechnology to develop crops with enhanced traits, such as improved nutrition.

To develop these crops, seed and agricultural companies have formed strategic alliances that combine technology -- such as how to implant genes in crops -- with companies that have extensive portfolios of genes.

"What we would envision happening is that other technology suppliers would want to be included in what we do over time and bring their traits and some of their products to the market place through what Pioneer and DuPont will do together," said Richard McConnell, senior vice president of research at Pioneer.

While agricultural companies hail biotechnology as a way of improving farm productivity, some groups have protested the advent of genetically altered crops. Greenpeace, for example, has sought to ban shipments of genetically altered soybeans in Europe.

"I think it's an education process," McConnell said of consumer fears about genetically altered crops. "We thoroughly test all of our products so we know and can predict how they are going to perform in the field."

The Pioneer-DuPont link follows other alliances in agriculture. Monsanto Co., for example, has a research alliance and a significant stake in DeKalb Genetics Corp., the No. 2 North American seed corn company.

DuPont said it expects to take a one-time, non-cash charge against its earnings of up to $1 billion as part of its investment in Pioneer. The charge is to write off research and development that is in process.
In addition to its biotechnology-based business, DuPont Agricultural Products supplies crop protection products, which are not part of the alliance.
The agreement includes a 16-year standstill and corporate governance agreement that will enable Pioneer to stay independent.

"There was some concern that they (Pioneer) might get taken over," Prudential's McMillin said. "DuPont will own 20 percent of the stock and insiders control at least that amount. In effect, the voting control of Pioneer will be held by insiders."
